content: An iodide ion is an iodine atom that carries a negative one (-1) charge. Compounds containing iodine in the formal oxidation state of -1 are referred to as iodides. These compounds can be either ionic, such as cesium iodide, or covalent, such as carbon tetraiodide. This naming convention is consistent with that used for chlorides and bromides. To chemically test for the presence of an iodide compound, the aqueous solution is first acidified by adding a few drops of acid to eliminate any carbonate ions. Following this, lead nitrate is introduced, resulting in the formation of a bright yellow precipitate of lead iodide. Most ionic iodides are soluble in water, with notable exceptions being yellow silver iodide and yellow lead iodide. Iron(III) iodide does not exist because iron(III) ions oxidize iodide ions in aqueous solutions. Aqueous solutions of iodide ions are more effective at dissolving iodine than pure water due to the formation of complex ions. The triiodide ion formed in this process imparts a brown color to the solution. Examples of Common Iodides: Hydrogen iodide (HI) Sodium iodide (NaI) Potassium iodide (KI) Carbon tetraiodide (CI₄) Silver iodide (AgI) Nitrogen triiodide (NI₃) Iodide as an Antioxidant and Clinical Use: Iodide, when administered in doses exceeding 6 mg per day, can be used to treat hyperthyroidism. This therapeutic effect is due to iodide's ability to inhibit the release of thyroid hormone (TH) from the thyroid gland, a phenomenon known as the Wolff-Chaikoff effect. Historically, prior to the 1940s, iodides were the primary antithyroid agents used in clinical practice. In large doses, iodides suppress the proteolysis of thyroglobulin, allowing thyroid hormone to be synthesized and stored in the colloid but preventing its release into the bloodstream. However, this treatment is rarely used as a standalone therapy today, despite the rapid improvement observed in patients immediately following administration. The primary drawback of iodide therapy is the accumulation of excessive stores of thyroid hormone, which delays the onset of action of thioamides (agents that block thyroid hormone synthesis). Additionally, the effectiveness of iodides diminishes after the initial treatment period. A phenomenon known as escape from block is also a concern, as the discontinuation of iodide therapy may lead to a sudden release of the stored thyroid hormone, causing a spike in its levels.
